Seafood / Contemporary

Doenjang-Glazed Grilled Black Cod

Rich black cod and the savory depth of doenjang, brought together over the grill.

Korean · Easy · Serves 4

Jump to recipe ↓
Chapter 02 / 15 seafood recipes ↗

Behind the dish

A PLACE AT
the table.

Stream: contemporary — the Korean answer to the miso cod. The famous miso-marinated black cod and this record share a fish and a technique family: a fermented bean paste cure, a long rest, and a slow sweet glaze under heat. The Korean version runs doenjang where the Japanese-American restaurant version runs miso — deeper, funkier, a shade less sweet — and the result is the same miracle from the other direction: buttery fish under a caramelized lacquer. Labeled honestly: this is a contemporary build, the pantry's oldest paste on a premium fish, and it is the site's special-occasion seafood record.

Set yourself up

Before you cook

  • The cure, 24–48 hours ahead, is the recipe. Whisk the cure's ingredients smooth and paint the fillets thickly on all faces; stack them in a dish, cover, refrigerate, turning once at the halfway mark. The paste's salt and enzymes work slowly into the flesh — at 24 hours the fish is seasoned; at 48 it is transformed, firm-silky and deeply savory. This is the one record on the site where "marinate longer" is always the right answer, and it is why the day-of work is fifteen minutes.
  • Decide the skin question before cooking: skin-on gives the crisp base and the fat's protection but shields the cure's contact; skin-off (this record's default for the full lacquer experience) wants a gentle touch and a moderate oven-or-grill path. Choose lacquer over crisp, or crisp over lacquer — both are correct, name the choice at the table.
  • Rinse or not: scrape the excess cure off the surface (leave the thin film that clings), but do not rinse the fillet — the rinse takes the cure's first two millimeters with it.
  • Fire for moderate and indirect-leaning: charcoal at medium with the fish offset, or a 200 °C oven finished under a hot broiler. The sugars caramelize over ten minutes; direct high heat takes them past caramel in two.

LET’S make it.

  1. 01
    Slow face first: skin-on goes skin-down, skin-off goes presentation-face-down, on the moderate zone. Six to eight minutes — the surface caramelizes slowly from paste-pale to tea-brown, and the fillet's underside sets. Checkpoint — the surface color reads deep tea with darker edges; the flesh at the sides has turned opaque a third of the way up. No black — black means the zone is running hot; offset further from the coals.
  2. 02
    Flip with a full spatula's support — black cod is soft as custard when raw and nearly as soft when cooked. Brush the caramelized first face with the finishing glaze, two minutes on the second side, glaze the second face, and pull at the flake stage: the flesh at the thickest point parts along the grain with a fork's weight and no force, still translucent-glossy at the very center (black cod's fat keeps it silky well past where other fish dry — around 55 °C internal at the center if you measure). Checkpoint — the test flake: sweet-savory lacquer outside, butter-fat silk inside, the doenjang's depth all the way through rather than sitting on the surface — that all-the-way-through is the 48-hour cure's signature, and no glaze trick can fake it.
  3. 03
    Sesame and scallion over, and serve in wide spoons or on rice — the fillet barely holds a shape. The sharp pickle beside every plate; the lacquer's sweetness and the pickle's acid are the plate's argument. Checkpoint — eating test: the first bite should be lacquer, silk, then the pickle's cut — the three-beat finish. If the pickle is an afterthought on the plate it will be an afterthought on the palate; this fish makes its own case for why Korean tables always set a sharp thing beside the rich one. Chef’s Note — on the cure's safety and keeping: salted at this ratio and refrigerated, the curing fish is comfortably good for 48 hours, and the tradition of fermented-paste fish curing in Korean kitchens (jeotgal-adjacent logic, salt preserving while enzymes work) is the ancestry the record leans on. Past 48 hours the texture heads toward firm-cured — a different, older dish that some tables love — but the sweet-spot window for lacquered grilled fillets is 24 to 48, and the record's clock stops there.

Doneness & Quality Checkpoints

  • The cure: 24–48 hours, turned once, excess scraped not rinsed.
  • The fire: moderate and offset; tea-brown caramel, never black.
  • The pull: parts at a fork's weight, translucent-glossy center — custard-soft, fully safe at the flake stage.
  • The plate: sharp pickle beside every serving; the richness is the foil, not the point.

Finish & Plate

One fillet per person on warm rice or a wide spoon, sesame and scallion over the lacquered face, the pickle plate passing. This is the seafood record that behaves like a main course — set it at the table's center and let the lacquer make the argument.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Lacquer burnt bitterDirect high heatModerate-offset; the 10-minute patience
Fish fell apart at the flipThin spatula, hard turnFull support, one confident motion
Flavor sits on the surfaceCure under 24 hoursThe full day minimum; 48 for the real thing
Too saltyDoenjang ran heavyScrape to the thin film; the finishing glaze balances
Fillets dry, not silkyOvercooked past the flake stagePull when it parts at a fork's weight

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

  • The cure is the keeping: curing fillets hold 48 hours (the clock above), cooked fish 2 days — cold flakes over rice with the thinned glaze is the day-after luxury.
  • Variations: the gochujang-glaze fork on the same cure clock (#SF10); the cure's logic on thick salmon at 12 hours; the scraped-off excess cure, simmered with a splash of water and strained, is a spoon-sauce for the platter — the zero-waste finish.
